title: Fastfire inference digest — rapid read + experiments
content:
Purpose: quickfire notes from recent reading + small experiment ideas to try this sprint. Not a formal write-up — mostly shorthand, TODOs, and mental models.

Top takeaways (high level):
- Prefix/KV cache interactions are the most underrated cost lever right now. Eviction policy + shard placement -> big perf delta for long-context workloads.
- Continuous batching heuristics matter more for tail-latency than mean throughput when request sizes are small and bursty.
- Low-bit quant can be surprisingly stable for many workloads but subtle prompt-sensitive regressions appear for retrieval-augmented prompts.

Papers skimmed (micro-summaries):
1) "Sparse-KV Sharding for Long-context Inference" (arXiv, link above) — key idea: shard KV by token-address ranges and allow overlapping reads during attention to reduce cross-GPU sync. Proto results show 1.2-1.6x throughput for 64k contexts on 8xA100. My note: need to check how this interacts with our current chunked KV layout. If we implement shallow overlap reads we might reduce RPCs but add memory duplication cost.

2) "Adaptive-batching with deadline-aware scheduling" — scheduling that prioritizes small low-latency requests and packs them opportunistically into batches before a deadline; reduces p95 by ~30ms at 200 qps. My note: could combine with route-based policies (hosted vs dedicated). Also think about a tiny on-node per-core queue with backpressure tokens.

3) "Quantization-induced prompt-sensitivity in RAG" — observed edge-case hallucination flares when embedding + quantized decoder interact. My note: run small eval with our internal prompt set (RAG-regen-20) to reproduce.

Quick experiment ideas (prioritized):
- E1: KV-overlap prototype (cheap sim)
  - goal: simulate cost of overlapping KV reads vs extra memory copy.
  - method: synthetic trace from prod (JIRA-INF-731 has a trace dump); emulate read amplification factor = 1.1..2.0.
  - metric: tokens/sec per GPU, additional peak memory, latency p95.
  - risk: traces may not capture real concurrency pattern.

- E2: Deadline-batch shim on CPU side
  - embed a 5ms deadline window for tiny requests, fall back to normal batching after.
  - quick perf harness: use wrk-like generator at 150 qps with mixed size distribution.
  - expected: p95 reduction, slight drop in mean throughput.

- E3: Low-bit RAG sensitivity check
  - take 200 RAG queries (RAG-regen-20), run against FP16 and int4 variants, compare logprob deltas and hallucination markers (precision/recall vs gold spans).
  - quick threshold: if token-level KL > 0.15 or span-F1 drops > 4%, flag for deeper eval.

Notes to self on implementation details:
- For KV overlap: need to map our KV layout (per-layer per-shard) to token-range indexes. Possible simple approach: keep original contiguous mapping and allow a 1-shard overlap window for tails. Implementation hack: when fetching, request neighboring shard slice if request extends > 75% into shard.
- For deadline batching: keep a small lock-free circular buffer per worker. Don't block the main reactor — use a lightweight timer wheel to flush.
- Logging: add per-request ledger tag: batch_path = {deadline|opportunistic|forced}, kv-reads = N, overlap = true/false. That will make offline analysis easier.

Rapid action items (this week):
- [ ] extract 1k long-context traces from S3 (ask infra for read-only export) — owner: Lena. (JIRA-INF-731)
- [ ] prototype CPU deadline shim on a dev box and run basic wrk script — owner: me (Theo)
- [ ] assemble RAG-regen-20 prompt set, run against current int8 build — owner: Maya

Open questions / things to think about:
- How much duplication memory budget can we afford on Dedicated nodes before customers complain? We should map to reserved GPU profile (e.g., 80GB) and calculate worst-case extra copy.
- Is there a quick way to do overlap reads without changing kernel code? Maybe via a light-weight copy that keeps data in pinned host memory and issues combined DMA? Not ideal but might be quick to test.
- Can we use model variants as graceful degradation: if overlap increases memory above threshold, route to smaller-ctx variant automatically? How to make rollback seamless for API users?

Useful links / references (scratch):
- Paper sim: https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.12345  (Sparse-KV Sharding)
- Prototype PR for batching shim: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/482
- Confluence note on shuffle/placement: confluence.redwood.com/display/INF/kv-sharding-notes

Random heuristics + heuristics to test quickly:
- If median request length < 64 tokens and > 70% of requests are < 128 tokens, bias to deadline-window = 3-5ms.
- Overlap width: start with 8k-token window (empiric), then measure hit-rate.

End-of-day micro-plan (what I will do right now):
1) draft small wrk script to emulate 100 qps mixed sizes (done in Python locally).
2) run a tiny end-to-end on a dev VM to confirm shape of p95 with and without deadline shim.
3) write short note in JIRA-INF-731 summarizing results and attach perf traces.

Notes-to-self: keep these short summaries in one file per sprint. If something looks promising, reformat into a proper RFC for eng-serving-runtime.

-- Theo
